source_text: Quantum ad philosophos, satis haec; quia quantum ad nostros, ex abundanti, quibus corporalitas animae in ipso Evangelio relucebit. Dolet apud inferos anima cujusdam, punitur in flamma, et cruciatur in lingua, et de digito animae felicioris implorat solatium roris. Imaginem existimas exitum illum pauperis laetantis et divitis moerentis? Et quid illic Lazari illic Lazari nomen, si non in veritate res est? Sed etsi imago credenda est, testimonium erit veritatis. Si enim non haberet anima corpus, non caperet imago animae imaginem corporis: nec mentiretur de corporalibus membris Scriptura, si non erant. Quid est autem illud quod ad inferna transfertur post divortium corporis? quod detinetur? quod in diem judicii reservatur? ad quod et Christus moriendo descendit? puto ad animas Patriarcharum. Sed quamobrem, si nihil anima sub terris? Nihil enim, si non corpus: incorporalitas enim ab omni genere custodiae libera est, immunis a poena et a fovela. Per quod enim punitur aut fovetur, hoc erit corpus; reddam de isto plenius et opportunius. Igitur si quid tormenti sive solatii anima praecerpit ia carcere seu diversorio inferum, in igni, vel in sinu Abrahae, probata erit corporalitas animae. Incorporalitas enim nihil patitur, non habens per quod pati possit: aut si habet, hoc erit corpus. In quantum enim omne corporale, passibile est; in tantum, quod passibile est, corporale est.
pass_a_gloss: As for philosophers, this is enough; because as for our own people, it will be clear from abundance, in that the corporality of the soul will shine forth in the Gospel itself. A certain soul grieves in the underworld, is punished in flame, and is tormented in the tongue, and from the finger of a happier soul it begs the solace of dew. Do you think that exit of the poor man rejoicing and the rich man mourning is an image? And what is the name of Lazarus there, if it is not a true thing? But even if the image is to be believed, it will be testimony to the truth. For if the soul did not have a body, it would not take on the image of the body: nor would Scripture lie about bodily members, if they were not. What is it, moreover, that is transferred to the underworld after the divorce of the body? What is detained? What is reserved until the day of judgment? To which also Christ, dying, descended? I think it is to the souls of the Patriarchs. But why, if the soul is nothing under the earth? For it is nothing, if not a body: for incorporeality is free from every kind of custody, immune from punishment and from heat. For through what it is punished or heated, this will be a body; I will give a fuller account of this later and more opportunely. Therefore, if the soul undergoes any torment or solace in the prison or lodging of the underworld, in fire, or in the bosom of Abraham, the corporality of the soul will be proven. For incorporeality suffers nothing, not having through which it can suffer: or if it has, this will be a body. Insofar as everything bodily is capable of suffering; insofar as it is capable of suffering, it is bodily.

choices.why: alternative to poena, to maintain consistency in translation

pass_b_english: I have said enough about the philosophers; for our own people, the corporality of the soul will become clear from the Gospel itself, and with plenty to spare. A certain soul grieves in the underworld, is punished in flame, and is tormented in the tongue, and it begs from the finger of a happier soul the solace of dew (Luke 16:19-31). Do you take that scene—the poor man rejoicing, the rich man mourning—to be a mere image? And what is Lazarus' name doing there, if it is not a true thing? But even if it is an image, it will serve as testimony to the truth. For if the soul did not have a body, it would not take on the image of a body; nor would Scripture lie about bodily members if they did not exist (Luke 16:19-31). What, then, is transferred to the underworld after the body's divorce? What is detained? What is reserved until the day of judgment? To which Christ also descended when he died—I mean to the souls of the Patriarchs (Luke 16:19-31). But why would he descend, if the soul is nothing under the earth? For it is nothing if it is not a body: incorporeality is free from every kind of custody, immune from punishment and from heat. Whatever it is through which a thing is punished or heated, that will be a body; I will give a fuller account of this later and at a better time. Therefore, if the soul undergoes any torment or solace in the prison or lodging of the underworld, in fire or in the bosom of Abraham, the corporality of the soul will be proven. For incorporeality suffers nothing, since it lacks that through which it could suffer; or if it has such a thing, that thing will be a body. Insofar as everything bodily is capable of suffering, to that extent what is capable of suffering is bodily.

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Latin text. Pass B includes necessary scripture citations (Luke 16:19-31) for the alluded passages, which is required by the instructions. The title 'The Soul's Corporality' correctly names the thought of the chapter.
